topStories.headline: SoMa's Rebuilt Gene Friend Rec Center Opens August 13 After Two-Year Closure
topStories.dek: The $59 million facility at 77 Harriet Street brings 25,000 square feet of new indoor recreation to one of the city's most park-starved neighborhoods.
topStories.body:
After more than two years without its only indoor recreational facility, South of Market is finally getting it back — and bigger. The new Gene Friend Recreation Center, now addressed at 77 Harriet Street, will hold its grand opening on Thursday, August 13, at 11:30 a.m., just as the San Francisco Unified School District school year begins.

The original facility at 270 Sixth Street closed for demolition in February 2024, leaving hundreds of children and teens without a trusted community space. The $59 million replacement — part of a broader citywide parks investment — is 50 percent larger than the building it replaces, clocking in at 25,000 square feet. The design by Mark Cavagnero Associates and Kuth Ranieri Architects features a gymnasium with two full-size basketball courts surrounded by expansive windows, a modern exercise area, two multi-purpose rooms, a kitchenette, and a new exterior playground accessible from an entry on Harriet Street.

All permitting agencies — Building, Electrical, Fire, Plumbing, and Accessibility — have signed off on the structure as safe to occupy, the San Francisco Recreation and Park Department announced. RPD used the month of July for final preparations before the public opening.

The project is part of a larger city commitment to open space equity in SoMa. In November 2024, Rec and Park also acquired the adjacent parcel at 240 Sixth Street — currently an auto repair shop under lease — for potential future expansion of outdoor recreational amenities in the neighborhood.

topStories.headline: Mission Bay Gets Its First Elementary School — 27 Years After It Was Promised
topStories.dek: Mission Bay Elementary School opens this month, the first new public elementary school built in San Francisco in more than a decade, serving the city's fastest-growing neighborhood.
topStories.body:
A promise made in the 1998 Mission Bay Redevelopment Plan is finally being kept. The San Francisco Unified School District is opening Mission Bay Elementary School in August 2026, located at the intersection of 6th Street and Mission Bay Boulevard South — the first new public elementary school to be built in the city in more than a decade.

The four-story, 81,800-square-foot building was made possible by Proposition A, which voters passed in 2016. It will initially serve pre-K through kindergarten during the 2026–27 school year before expanding one grade at a time, eventually enrolling more than 400 students. The fourth floor will also house the Mission Bay Hub, a program drawing students from six high schools across the city into STEM career pathways.

The school's architect, Chris McGiff-Brown, designed the space around what he calls 'Universal Design for Learning': wide, movable glass doors that can combine classrooms and workspaces into flexible learning environments. The attendance area for the new school encompasses SoMa, Mission Bay, Potrero Hill, and Dogpatch — the same zone currently served by Daniel Webster Elementary School, with both schools sharing the area tiebreaker.

The opening comes even as SFUSD grapples with roughly 14,000 empty seats districtwide and declining enrollment projections. Supporters say Mission Bay's explosive residential growth over the past three decades — which brought UCSF's campus, Chase Center, and the headquarters of OpenAI and Visa to the neighborhood — created a genuine need for local school capacity that the enrollment data alone doesn't capture.

topStories.headline: Planning Department Poised to Approve Prologis Mega-Project at Caltrain's 4th & King Railyards
topStories.dek: The 20-acre redevelopment plan by Prologis and Caltrain would bring 2,500 homes and an 850-foot tower to a site that currently divides SoMa from Mission Bay.
topStories.body:
San Francisco's Planning Department is moving toward approving one of the city's most ambitious post-pandemic development proposals: a 20-acre master-planned community on the Caltrain railyards at Fourth and King streets in South of Market, submitted by logistics giant Prologis in March 2026.

The proposal calls for between 7 and 8 million square feet at full buildout, including approximately 4 million square feet of commercial office space and roughly 2,500 housing units. At the heart of the project is an 850-foot mixed-use tower that would rise directly above a rebuilt, 'world-class' Caltrain station — which would remain operational throughout construction.

The Potrero View reported in June 2026 that the Planning Department was poised to approve the application, with the city having published a complete application notice establishing a mid-June decision deadline. If approved, Prologis says Caltrain would begin upgrading rail infrastructure before tower construction commences. Full buildout is contingent on identifying an offsite location for rail storage and on completion of the Portal downtown rail extension project.

Beyond housing and offices, the redeveloped site would open a promenade on Townsend Street, a public plaza on 5th Street, and a public park on 6th Street. The site is also identified as a future gateway station for California High-Speed Rail. Supporters say the project would physically stitch together SoMa, Showplace Square, and Mission Bay — neighborhoods currently separated by the sprawling active railyard.

moreNews.headline: Mission Creek Boathouse Reopens Under Dogpatch Paddle for Giants Games and Youth Programs
moreNews.body: After an eight-month closure, the Mission Creek Boathouse at 401 Berry Street is back in operation, now run by Dogpatch Paddle under a new agreement with the San Francisco Recreation and Park Department. The operator is offering kayak and paddleboard rentals, lessons, tours, private events, and youth programming. A special feature is game-day kayak packages allowing paddlers to watch San Francisco Giants home games from McCovey Cove. The boathouse also serves as a second site for Dogpatch Paddle's after-school and summer youth camps. Paddlers can eventually opt for a one-way trip between Mission Creek and the primary Crane Cove Park location at 701 Illinois Street, timed with the tides.

moreNews.headline: SoMa West Neighborhood Association Filed State Complaint Over 'Hyper-Concentration of Poverty'
moreNews.body: The SoMa West Neighborhood Association, representing more than 200 city residents, filed a formal complaint earlier this year with the California Department of Housing and Community Development and the California Attorney General's Office, alleging that San Francisco has illegally concentrated homeless resources and affordable housing in the South of Market neighborhood. The complaint argues the arrangement violates state housing law and civil rights mandates. Association board member Shaun Aukland stated that while SoMa houses only 11 percent of the city's unhoused population, the neighborhood hosts 28 percent of the city's shelter beds. The city's Office of Economic and Workforce Development noted that the Office of Homelessness and Supportive Housing awarded Abode Property Management $734,827 annually for SoMa Ambassadors.

moreNews.headline: Potrero Power Station Block 2 Foundation Work Underway as UCSF Cancer Research Building Rises
moreNews.body: Construction crews are actively working on the foundation for Block 2 of the Potrero Power Station redevelopment on San Francisco's central waterfront in Dogpatch — a seven-story complex designed by Herzog & de Meuron that will become a UCSF cancer research center. Developer Fifth Space (formerly Associate Capital) also saw the opening of the Sophie Maxwell affordable housing building in October 2025, an eight-story corten steel-clad building delivering 105 units of permanently affordable housing for households earning 50–110% of area median income. The broader Potrero Power Station master plan envisions a 5.3 million square foot mixed-use community with more than 2,600 homes, 1.6 million square feet of commercial and lab space, a 250-room hotel, and nearly 7 acres of open space.
